questions.prompt: For each species, identify whether it is neutral or charged and whether it has an unpaired electron: Na⁺, NH₄⁺, Cl•, and [M]•⁺ formed when a molecule loses one electron in mass spectrometry. Then state the precise difference between an isotope pair and an ion pair of the same element.
hints: Charge comes from unequal numbers of protons and electrons; a dot has a distinct meaning.
An isotope keeps the same atomic number.

questions.prompt: Chlorine has isotope masses 34.969 and 36.966. Its average atomic mass is 35.45. (a) Calculate the fraction and percent of ³⁷Cl. (b) Explain why the average molecular mass of CH₂Cl₂ is not itself a single peak in its mass spectrum; name the three isotope-combination masses that produce the cluster.
hints: Let y be the ³⁷Cl fraction and 1−y the ³⁵Cl fraction.
A mass spectrum records discrete isotope combinations, not a weighted mean.

questions.prompt: Use these average bond dissociation energies: H–H 436 kJ/mol, F–F 155 kJ/mol, H–F 565 kJ/mol. (a) Calculate Δ = BDEHF − √(BDEHH×BDEFF). (b) Use Δχ = 0.102√Δ to estimate the electronegativity difference. (c) Explain why breaking an H–F bond has positive ΔH but forming it has negative ΔH.
hints: Keep Δ in kJ/mol before applying the 0.102 relationship.
Bond breaking and bond forming have opposite energy directions.

(a) Identify which peak is the molecular ion and estimate the number of carbon atoms from the second peak. (b) Propose a chemically valid hydrocarbon formula with molecular mass 70 and calculate its degree of unsaturation. (c) State one structural class consistent with the result.

questions.prompt: For HCl, μ = 1.08 D and R = 1.27 Å. (a) Draw the course-convention bond-dipole arrow and label δ+ and δ−. (b) Calculate the partial charge fraction using δ = μ(3.336×10⁻²⁰)/(1.602×10⁻¹⁹R). (c) Explain why this result does not make HCl an ionic compound with full ±1 charges.
hints: The course arrow runs from δ+ toward the more electronegative atom.
A fraction such as 0.18 is a partial charge, not a count of electrons transferred.

questions.prompt: An unknown organic compound has a very broad absorption spanning roughly 2500–3300 cm⁻¹, a strong sharp absorption near 1710 cm⁻¹, and a strong feature in the 1000–1300 cm⁻¹ region. (a) Identify the most supported functional-group class. (b) Explain why an ester is a weaker answer despite also having C=O and C–O. (c) State how the shape of the broad feature relates to intermolecular interactions.
hints: Use all three observations together.
Compare which candidate contains an O–H bond.

questions.prompt: A student says “n + 1 tells me the number of NMR signals.” Correct this statement. Then, for (CH₃)₂CHBr, (a) predict the number of unique proton environments and their integrations, and (b) predict the splitting of the methyl environment and the methine environment using the course n + 1 rule.
hints: First use symmetry to count environments; only then apply splitting within each environment.
The methyl groups are equivalent, and each one is adjacent to the one methine H.

questions.prompt: An unknown gives an M:M+2 pair in a 1:1 ratio at m/z 122 and 124, a strong mass-spectral fragment at m/z 43, and an IR spectrum with no broad O–H or C=O absorption. (a) State the first structural conclusion from the high-mass pair and propose a formula consistent with the 122 peak and the m/z 43 fragment. (b) Explain why m/z 43 is chemically plausible. (c) Name the next measurement from this unit that would most directly tell you how many distinct hydrogen environments the proposed molecule has, and list the three evidence types you would read from that measurement.
hints: Start from the isotope pattern before trying formulas.
One halogen’s mass and a common alkyl cation can account for the key numbers.
